post1.text:
Hiring executives is not a growth strategy. It is a bet.

Companies scaling past $50M often confuse adding senior talent with building leadership capacity. They are not the same thing. When CleanCapital recently restructured its entire executive team to support platform scale, they were not just filling seats. They were making a calculated architectural decision about how the company would operate at its next level.

Here is what leaders at this stage consistently get wrong:

1. They hire for the company they have, not the company they are becoming. A VP who thrived at $20M often stalls at $80M.

2. They treat leadership transitions as HR events rather than strategic ones. Every executive change reshapes how decisions get made across the entire organization.

3. They underestimate the cost of misalignment at the top. One wrong hire in the C-suite does not slow growth by 10%. It can stop it entirely.

The leaders who scale successfully treat their executive team like a living system, not a fixed org chart.

Who on your current leadership team was built for where you are going, not just where you have been?

post2.text:
A recent piece in citybiz covered CleanCapital's decision to reshape its entire executive team as it works to scale its solar and storage platform.

Most people read that as an energy sector story. We read it as a scaling story.

When a company restructures leadership to support growth, it is rarely about the individuals leaving or arriving. It is about recognizing that the organizational design that got you here will not get you there. That is a hard truth for founders and CEOs to sit with.

At Autobahn, we work with companies navigating exactly this moment. The $50M to $500M range is where leadership architecture either becomes your greatest accelerator or your biggest bottleneck.

If your executive team has not changed as fast as your revenue has, that gap is worth examining.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxNWWJYVV83U0lvX2xxQWtKRUtiVE1lUERRd1pEN2MyU1BodHItU2tJVzJyOV9mSXRjM0M1TFhMMjdYamFoWDVYU2Nwdy1iQjRTSjFqR0FfWWdLNGRqZTBFbFJBUkxtQ21GLWQ1V082elZrcV8wV2ZjZ3VkM3lSSUdMM2ZDSUtqVnZaQ0R1anpQMllSU1JLUk1tWE01dENROWlSQlJNNk1lUkVJcmZLbWZkZQ

post3.text:
When CleanCapital restructured its executive team to support platform scale, they were living out a principle Katherine Slain writes about directly in Chapter 1 of our upcoming book.

The chapter is called Lead Like Lives Depend On It.

The title is not hyperbole. Katherine makes the case that at the $50M to $500M growth stage, leadership decisions carry consequences that most executives are not fully accounting for. The people you put in the room, the decisions you give them authority to make, and the culture you build through your own daily behavior determine whether your company scales or stalls.

One insight she surfaces early: the standard of leadership required to grow does not rise gradually. It jumps. And most leaders are not prepared for how personal that demand becomes.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Your exit is not a finish line. It is a destination you should have been navigating toward for years before you ever sit across from a buyer.

Most business leaders at the $50M+ level treat exit planning as an event. Buyers treat it as a report card on everything you have or have not done.

A recent piece in Entrepreneur confirmed what we see constantly: founders who grow successfully still get caught off guard at the table because they never aligned their operations, financials, and leadership structure with what acquirers actually value.

Here is what changes when you plan earlier:

Your EBITDA multiple expands when revenue is predictable and not founder-dependent. Buyers pay a premium for documented processes, not tribal knowledge. Customer concentration above 20% in a single account is a valuation haircut waiting to happen.

The companies that command the highest multiples are not necessarily the fastest growers. They are the most acquirable.

So here is the question worth sitting with: If a serious buyer reviewed your business today, what would kill the deal?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes on the essential elements of successful exit planning makes a point we see validated with clients every quarter: most business owners start thinking about their exit far too late to actually shape their outcome.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M toward $500M and beyond. At that stage, the decisions you make about leadership depth, recurring revenue, and financial reporting quality are not just operational choices. They are valuation choices.

The companies that exit on their terms are the ones that spent two to three years before the transaction making their business look exactly the way a sophisticated buyer wants to see it.

If you are scaling and have not started thinking about your multiple, you are already behind. Read the Forbes piece here and then let us know what you are seeing in your own planning process.

post3.text:
Exit planning conversations tend to start with the wrong question. Most owners ask: what is my business worth? The better question is: what would make a buyer pay significantly more than that?

Chapter 2 of Rock Your Business, titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, is written by Paul Belair and George Hohman, two practitioners who have been inside these transactions. They lay out exactly how companies in the $50M to $500M range can close the gap between what they think they are worth and what a buyer will actually put on the table.

One thing the chapter makes clear: your multiple is not set by the market. It is set by decisions you make long before a deal is ever discussed. The variables are more controllable than most founders realize.

Rock Your Business, the follow-up to Rock the Recession by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, is releasing soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most business owners spend years building a company and about six months thinking about how to sell it. That gap is exactly where value gets left on the table. The multiple a buyer puts on your business is not a market accident. It is the result of decisions made years before you ever enter a deal room. Here is what scaling companies need to understand now.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does because it worked before. A strategy is a deliberate system designed for where you're going, not where you've been.

Gartner's recent research on AI and sales productivity makes this painfully clear: companies are investing in tools that save time, but that saved time isn't converting to revenue. Why? Because there's no strategy directing what to do with it.

Here's what scaling companies need to confront:

1. Activity metrics are not sales strategy. Volume without direction is noise.
2. Your best reps succeeding is not proof your system works. It may just mean your best reps are saving you from your system.
3. Time saved by technology only compounds results when there's a defined playbook to point it at.

The $50M to $500M jump doesn't happen because you sell harder. It happens because you stop improvising.

What does your sales strategy actually prescribe, and when did you last pressure-test it?

post2.text:
A recent piece from McKinsey on the economics of B2B growth put a number to something we see constantly with scaling companies: the gap between businesses that grow past a certain threshold and those that plateau is widening, and the difference is rarely the product.

It comes down to commercial discipline. Companies that thrive past $100M have tighter alignment between their growth strategy and how their sales organization actually operates day to day.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams who are often shocked to discover their sales motion was built for a $20M company. It still feels familiar, so nobody questions it.

If your revenue has scaled but your sales structure has not, that gap is costing you more than you think.

Read the full McKinsey piece here and then ask yourself whether your sales strategy was designed for where you are or where you started: https://news.google.

post3.text:
A recent report highlighted that B2B sales teams adopting AI and personalization are pulling ahead fast, while those without a clear strategy are simply falling behind.

Chapter 4 of Rock Your Business addresses this directly. The chapter is titled Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation, and it was written by Deb and Brandon for exactly this reason: most leadership teams at growing companies assume they have a sales strategy when what they actually have is a collection of individual habits held together by top performers.

One of the core ideas in the chapter is that a real sales strategy has to be teachable, repeatable, and independent of any single person on your team. If it leaves when your best rep does, it was never a strategy.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is not the colors on your website. Your brand is what people feel when they interact with your company, and most $50M+ businesses have no idea what that feeling actually is.

JBL recently shifted its entire marketing approach away from campaigns and toward cultural identity. The result is a brand that people belong to, not just buy from. That distinction matters more than most executives realize.

Here is what scaling companies consistently get wrong about branding:

First, they confuse awareness with identity. Getting your name out there means nothing if people cannot tell you apart from three competitors.

Second, they treat marketing as a department instead of a discipline that runs through every customer touchpoint.

Third, they build campaigns for quarters instead of building a brand for decades.

At the $50M to $500M stage, you have enough momentum to make real brand decisions. The question is whether you are making them intentionally or by accident.

What does your company actually stand for, and would your customers say the same thing you would?

#BrandStrategy #ScalingBusiness #MarketingLeadership

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive on Ulta's CMO caught our attention. The core idea is that Ulta is not choosing between brand building and performance marketing. They are running both simultaneously across every channel their customers use.

That balance is exactly where scaling companies struggle.

Most businesses between $50M and $500M default to performance marketing because it is measurable and the board loves the numbers. Brand building feels softer, slower, harder to defend in a quarterly review. So it gets deprioritized, and the company grows revenue without growing a real brand.

The companies that break through to $500M and beyond figure out that brand equity is a growth asset, not a marketing expense.

If you are navigating that tension right now, this article is worth your time.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE?oc=5

post3.text:
JBL made a deliberate choice to stop marketing around campaigns and start marketing around culture. For growing companies, that shift is harder than it sounds, and most leaders do not know where to begin.

Chapter 5 of our upcoming book Rock Your Business is titled 'What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?' Chapter authors Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West tackle exactly this problem. They work with companies at the $50M to $500M stage who have outgrown their original brand story but have not built a new one.

One insight they share: your brand has a scent whether you designed it or not. The real question is whether the smell is attracting the right customers or quietly driving them away.

That framing alone tends to change how leadership teams talk about marketing.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

Between $50M and $500M, the companies that scale fastest are not the ones spending more on marketing. They are the ones who finally got clear on what their brand actually stands for and built everything else around that.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a cost strategy dressed up as ambition.

SHRM's latest research on 2026 hiring trends makes this clear: the companies winning the talent game are not casting the widest nets. They are getting surgical about exactly who they need and why before a single job description gets written.

For leaders scaling past $50 million, that shift matters enormously. Three things worth internalizing:

First, headcount growth and organizational growth are not the same thing. Confusing the two is expensive.

Second, hiring precision starts with role clarity. If your team cannot define what success looks like in a role 90 days in, you are not ready to hire for it.

Third, your best talent decisions happen before the interview. The filters you set upstream determine the quality of every conversation downstream.

At the growth stage, one wrong senior hire can cost you 18 months of momentum. One right one can compress your timeline by the same amount.

So here is the question: Does your current hiring process reflect the company you are building, or the company you were two years ago?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM on 2026 hiring trends caught our attention. The core finding: high-growth companies are shifting from volume-based recruiting to precision-based recruiting, focusing on fewer, better-defined roles rather than expanding headcount broadly.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is not a trend to watch. It is a warning to act on now.

At this stage, every hire either accelerates your trajectory or complicates it. There is rarely a neutral outcome. The organizations that scale well treat talent acquisition as a strategic function, not an HR function. That distinction changes everything from who owns the process to how decisions get made.

If your talent strategy still looks like it did when you were a $20M company, it is time for a reset.

Read the full SHRM piece here and tell us what resonates: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMioAFBVV95cUxPRFVYR0VscXJpMmVqV2dwazJDTkstVDJTNG9uTlZlWHJPVkFqQ0MzZTRQSUYwUDZweWw2dE52THZKSnhBTzQtb1g5UUYzbmJTbjFJcXlVYno2ZzU4aU0yNVRwN2RIN05xTWJVWnZQejVyY2xRNmJ2SF83QmVHel9GYmdWTEdEMWZLMVk5OThMNTF0TmdKR1F4bG84cnZRZ0FU?oc=5

post3.text:
The conversation around precision hiring is everywhere right now, and for good reason. But knowing you need to hire smarter and knowing how to build the system that makes it happen consistently are two very different problems.

Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business, titled The Talent Engine, addresses exactly that gap. Written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, this chapter goes beyond hiring philosophy and gets into the operating mechanics that scaling companies actually need.

One idea worth sitting with before you read it: your talent process is only as strong as the clarity you have about where your business is going. Most companies at this growth stage are hiring for today and accidentally slowing down tomorrow.

There is a better way to build the engine.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams at $50M+ companies are not suffering from a lack of data. They are drowning in it. A recent Business.com breakdown of KPI tracking tools highlights just how many options exist to capture and display metrics. The tools are not the problem. The selection of what to measure is.

Here is what high-performing scaling companies do differently:

1. They limit leadership dashboards to five to seven metrics that directly connect to the company's critical priorities for the year. Not the department. The company.

2. They treat lagging indicators as scorecards and leading indicators as steering wheels. Most teams only watch the scoreboard after the game is over.

3. They review their KPI set quarterly. Metrics that made sense at $50M can become noise at $150M.

Tracking everything feels productive. It rarely is.

If you stripped your dashboard down to the six numbers that actually drive your growth, would your team know what they are?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Oracle NetSuite outlines 30 financial metrics and KPIs companies should consider tracking heading into 2026. It is a thorough list and worth a read.

But here is what the list does not tell you: for a company scaling from $50M toward $500M, a long list of metrics is often the enemy of focus.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern consistently. Leadership teams add KPIs as the business grows, and nobody ever removes them. The result is a dashboard nobody trusts and a leadership team arguing about data instead of acting on it.

The question is not which 30 metrics you could track. It is which 6 you must track right now.

Read the full Oracle NetSuite article here and use it as a filter, not a checklist: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMikwFBVV95cUxNcThuZllxNkVka0dpOV9QdHZQM2RiU0tfMGVIR05tdW9ZN1AtYngwQ1d4WDFSb3ZNSUxKNHFCSUR4aC1lR1g2ZWYzWFE0NWF1WmVpejAxOW9VRFdJa01yLUFKa1hvbjNGQnR6a2hZcVVtQzgwRXNCdXVGbjhfNWR2eWpTSlFyRk5zLVZ3MnJvMU14ZjA

post3.text:
CliftonLarsonAllen recently published a guide on KPIs for manufacturers looking to improve company performance. Good timing. This conversation is one we have seen play out in boardrooms across industries, not just manufacturing.

In Chapter 7 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, co-authored by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, the chapter is titled Death by KPIs for a reason. The authors work with leadership teams that have built elaborate measurement systems and still cannot answer the one question that matters: are we winning or losing right now, and why?

One thing the chapter makes clear is that the number of KPIs a company tracks tends to grow with headcount, but accountability does not automatically grow with it. That gap is where performance starts to break down.

Rock Your Business — available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most companies are failing at AI not because the technology is bad, but because they handed it to the wrong people and called it a strategy.

A recent survey found that 90% of executives report AI has not meaningfully improved productivity at their organizations. And yet, many of those same leaders are still cutting headcount in the name of AI-driven efficiency. That is not transformation. That is cost-cutting wearing a disguise.

Here is what scaling companies get wrong:

First, AI adoption without workflow redesign is just expensive distraction. The tool does not fix a broken process.

Second, productivity gains from AI accrue to people who already know how to work well. If your team is struggling before AI, AI will not save them.

Third, the leaders seeing real returns are treating AI as a thinking partner, not a task-executor. That requires a fundamentally different implementation mindset.

If 90% of executives are disappointed, what does that tell you about how your industry is measuring success in the first place?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune reported that 90% of executives say AI has not boosted productivity at their companies. Some are still reducing staff anyway, betting on future gains that have not materialized yet.

For companies scaling between $50M and $500M, this is a five-alarm warning.

At that stage, your operational margin for error is thin. Cutting people based on AI promises you cannot yet measure is not bold leadership. It is a liability.

The companies winning with AI right now are not replacing people wholesale. They are identifying specific, high-friction workflows and deploying AI with precision. That requires honest internal assessment before any investment decision.

Before your next AI initiative, ask your team one question: what problem, exactly, are we solving?

Read the full Fortune piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMifEFVX3lxTE5LZWF5Vkc3Wk9DVVd5aE83ZGVhbWMyb3U3MW1kcHljOHdwcjdjTmt1SmU5bFVRblVaZGJsRndNRS1fWExxc3IyZDBJcnlxZHhYVUFhV1pBSzVRS0R1RVJlNVYxM0pzRXZKcG96RExTdTVlMnhBWDNMUlVuUGM?oc=5

post3.text:
Ninety percent of executives say AI has not improved productivity. That number would not surprise Hudson Shank or Jonathan Slain.

In Chapter 8 of our upcoming book Rock Your Business, titled The Third Monitor Theory, Hudson and Jonathan make a case that most leaders are thinking about AI adoption at entirely the wrong level. The issue is not access to tools. It is the absence of a deliberate framework for where AI actually fits inside a scaling organization's decision-making structure.

The Third Monitor Theory reframes how executives at $50M to $500M companies should position AI in their daily operations. Not as a replacement layer, and not as a novelty, but as something far more specific and far more powerful.

The insight is simple once you see it. But most leadership teams are not looking in the right place.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to derail your company's growth are not the incompetent ones. They are the capable ones who secretly believe they do not belong.

Imposter syndrome does not disappear when you hit $50M in revenue. Forbes Australia recently reported that high achievers carry self-doubt all the way to the top, and in many cases, success actually intensifies it. The bigger the title, the louder the voice that says you do not deserve it.

For leaders scaling toward $500M, this matters in three concrete ways:

1. Self-doubt slows decisions. Leaders who question their legitimacy hesitate when speed is the competitive advantage.

2. It creates cultures of silence. When the person at the top performs confidence instead of practicing it, the whole team stops raising problems early.

3. It gets expensive. Talented executives leave companies where the leadership psychology is fractured, even when the strategy is sound.

The question worth sitting with: Is your leadership team making bold moves, or are they managing appearances?

#Leadership #ExecutiveDevelopment #BusinessGrowth

post2.text:
A recent piece in Seattle University outlines six practical ways leaders can overcome imposter syndrome when stepping into a new role. The advice is solid for individuals. But for companies scaling past $50M, the stakes are organizational, not just personal.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly. A company promotes a strong operator into a senior leadership role. That leader spends the first six months managing their own self-doubt instead of driving growth. The business stalls. Not because of strategy. Because of psychology.

Identifying and addressing imposter syndrome in your leadership team is not a soft skill exercise. It is a scaling imperative.

If you are building leaders for the next stage of growth, this article is worth your time.

How could you be that successful and still not feel like you belong there?

That question sits at the center of Chapter 9 in our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond. The chapter, titled How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?, was authored by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo.

What they uncovered is not what most leadership books tell you. Imposter syndrome at the executive level is not a confidence problem. It is a structural problem, and it shows up in how decisions get made, how teams get led, and how growth gets blocked.

Samantha, Caleb, and Rafa offer a framework for diagnosing it in yourself and in your organization before it costs you momentum.

post1.text:
The most dangerous blind spot for a $50M+ business leader is not a market shift or a talent gap. It is the complete absence of a personal life plan.

Most founders have a five-year growth roadmap. Almost none have a five-year personal roadmap sitting next to it. A recent Entrepreneur piece confirmed what we see constantly: founders who plan obsessively for business growth almost never plan for what comes after, or alongside, it.

Three things scaling leaders consistently overlook:

1. Your role in the business will need to change before you are ready for it to. Design that transition now, not when the pressure forces it.

2. Revenue milestones are not identity milestones. Know the difference before the business hits $200M and you still feel empty.

3. The people closest to you are running a parallel experience of your growth story. They deserve a seat in the planning process.

You have a strategic plan for the company. Do you have one for your life?

#LeadershipDevelopment #BusinessGrowth #WorkLifeDesign

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, in partnership with Morgan Stanley, lays out a sobering reality: most entrepreneurs have no structured plan for life after a liquidity event. The financial mechanics get attention. The identity crisis that follows does not.

At Autobahn, we work with leaders scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond, and the pattern is consistent. The closer a company gets to a major transition, the less the founder has thought about what they personally want on the other side of it.

That gap is not a wealth management problem. It is a life design problem, and it needs to be solved before the term sheet lands on the table.

If you are building toward an exit or a major inflection point, start planning the personal side now. Read the Fortune piece for context, then let's talk.

post3.text:
Founders obsess over scaling the business. Almost no one builds an intentional plan for scaling their life alongside it.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, was written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain, and it tackles exactly this. The chapter challenges leaders at the $50M to $500M stage to stop treating personal life planning as something to do after the next milestone.

One insight that stops readers cold: the moment you most need to invest in your personal life design is usually the exact moment your business demands make it feel impossible. That tension is not accidental. It is the signal.

This chapter does not offer a work-life balance formula. It offers a framework for building a life you actually want to return to when you come up for air.
